newsitem.title: FINLAND: FOCUS - UPM-Kymmene frees up cash. [CORRECTED 14:38 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UPM-Kymmene frees up cash. [CORRECTED 14:38 GMT]

text.p: UPM-Kymmene, Europe's largest forestry group, looks to be on the acquisition trail, analysts said on Thursday after the company said it sold a large chunk of shares in telecoms group Nokia for a 1.5 billion markka ($291 million) gain.

UPM, on the record as saying its main short-term goal is reducing debts, said it would use cash generated on the sale of 4.5 million Nokia A shares to improve its balance sheet. The bourse said the price was 385.10-385.20 markka per share.
"This is to reduce debt which is well-known as our central target," Chief Financial Officer Jan-Henrik Kulp said by telephone. But he added the company does not earmark funds for any specific use.

Analysts welcomed the share sale as a clear signal the Finnish forestry group is moving to liquefy some of the assets marked in its balance sheet at well below market value, noting it would also make financing a purchase easier for UPM.
"It could well be because of a potential acquisition in the U.S. market that they wanted to do something now," said Dennis Christie at Morgan Stanley in London.

The timing of UPM's sale of Nokia stock -- to U.S. brokerage Goldman Sachs for re-offering internationally -- was well-timed coming on Wednesday with Nokia at all-time highs, over 390 markka. Its book value for UPM was 40 markka.

On the debt issue, one analyst requesting anonymity calculated that UPM's divestments so far -- including deconsolidation of Rauma -- may be able to lift its equity to assets ratio to above 45 percent, from 41 percent at end-March.
UPM's own target is a ratio of at least 40 percent.
Analysts said UPM has made clear that it is seeking an acquisition of either a business or a paper plant in North America, partly to balance its currency exposure.
"Their two top priorities are growth in North America and taking part in the restructuring of the fine paper industry in Europe," said Lars Kjellberg at Credit Suisse First Boston in London.

But analysts differed on whether UPM would sell off more Nokia stock: this week's sale still left it with 7.1 million Nokia shares, which at current market prices could bring in another 2.8 billion markka.
"It's more a question of timing," said Jacob Nyman at Evli Securities. "Over some sort of time period I think they will sell the rest -- maybe within a year's time."
But one analyst thought Finland's intimate corporate culture, with cross-relationships between companies at supervisory board level, made an out-and-out sale improbable.

Various possibilities exist for UPM in North America, analysts said: the most obvious is debt-laden Repap Enterprises, which said on Wednesday it was reviewing bids for its operating units, and in which UPM has expressed interest.
But they stressed UPM will only move at the right price -- the company pledged in its annual report that it would be careful in planning capital outlays and investment.
In Europe, Christie said it would not fit UPM's strategy of North American growth to buy a major stake in Swedish Stora, as a Swedish newspaper speculated may happen.
Another analyst said Stora as an acquisition target was "far-fetched, but a possibility." UPM's Kulp said he had "no idea what this (speculation) is all about".
Analysts said the main names in the European fine-paper frame are Swedish SCA and Dutch KNP BT as divestors, with potential buyers UPM and Stora.
"Everybody seems to be waiting for the first step to be taken," said Kjellberg.

UPM could also release more capital by selling all or some of its shares in Finnish forestry group Enso, analysts said: at current prices its 10 million or so shares could deliver about 480 million (corrects from 4.8 billion )markka. ($ = 5.151 Finnish Markka)
